title: Brass bands, parades and the Humphreys
summary: Lee describes cutting contests and parade playing, the Tuxedo band, funeral marches and forming a band with the Humphreys, then Eddie Jackson's job.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: So Bill, so Bill playing that corner, really was my life. I lived that life, I lived that life and I loved it. Well, what you really got yourself a reputation playing corner in New Orleans was playing in the brass bands, parades. On those parades, you met everybody and the corner players all had their cutting contests. So, I played in the brass band, in Black Penny's brass band with Louis, Renee and myself, regular. And later years, I worked with the Tuxedo band with Papa Celestan. That's where I got, come and get some of my best technique of good old funeral marches we used to play. Good old funeral marches and then, and then, every six eighths, like, Gettysburg march, you know, for the parades and everything. In those days, everybody second line and picked out their band, who they liked, who they liked, who they liked to be and then, and you got famous by that. It's a funny thing, you played in an orchestra, people paid no attention to you, but as soon you hit that street, everybody had their eyes on you, you know, especially those good play cornets. They didn't watch nobody but the cornets and the drums and the clarinet. So, I got to work with a boyfriend of mine, I'm raised up with, Boy Lumprey. Lumprey boys. One of them was a drummer, a poise lady, a lady come to be a cornered player, I helped him out, his grandfather taught him, grandfather taught me a while, the music too. Then Willie Humphrey Client, so, we mix up a band, we mix up a band together, and we played around together a long time, we went to the old Avila dance hall, when I was built between McGonagall and Rampart, next to the 4N, that little Eddie Miller, the Client, Eddie Miller, the saxophone player, he used to play, he used to come in and sit in with me every night there. Then I, I went to work at Canal and Crotlet, with the bass tuba player of the Tuxedo Brass band, Eddie Jackson. Stayed up there a long while playing cornered. One of the greatest things of my life, around 1924 I got a letter from Joe, Joe, Joe Oliver. Yeah, Preston Jackson and, uh, and uh, we tell that boy played drum, play trombone Mary, come here and see me. You got to tell me little brother Montgomery?
They all went. They all went.
